claim: The recombinantly produced proteins did not co-purify with any lipids from the expression host.
source: In contrast, neither the 4-monomethyl sterol, the 4,4-dimethyl sterol, nor any other lipids were present when the proteins were incubated with the DMSO negative control, suggesting that the recombinantly produced proteins did not co-purify with any lipids from the expression host.

claim: The average equilibrium dissociation constant for BstAPD binding to 4-monomethyl sterol was determined to be 4.41±0.14 μM with a Hill coefficient of 4.0.

claim: BstAPD and BstB exhibit cooperativity for binding to 4-monomethyl substrate, indicating that multiple binding sites are plausible.
source: Additionally, BstAPD and BstB exhibit cooperativity for binding to 4-monomethyl substrate, indicating that multiple binding sites are plausible.

source: The MST results revealed no interaction between BstAPD and BstB with either cholesterol or lanosterol.

claim: BstC bound to lanosterol with a Kd value of 17.3±3.92 μM.

evidence: This is based on MST experimental data.

claim: BstC is more tolerant to non-native substrates than BstAPD and BstB.

evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data showing BstC binds cholesterol and lanosterol while the others do not.

claim: The 1.6 Å-resolution structure of BstB was determined by experimental phasing.
source: The 1.6 Å-resolution structure of was determined by experimental phasing, producing electron density that allowed the unambiguous building of a model of BstB (except for one disordered loop spanning residues 202–204).
evidence: This describes the crystallographic structure determination.

claim: The BstB structure comprises two globular α/β domains that form a cleft at the middle.
source: The structure comprises two globular α/β domains (Figure 4A, domains A and B) that form a cleft at the middle.
evidence: This describes the structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Domain A of BstB contains six β-strands while domain B contains five.
source: Domain A contains six β-strands while domain B contains five.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: All the β-strands in BstB are flanked by α-helices.
source: All the β-strands are flanked by αhelices.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The two domains of BstB are connected by two loops: one 9-residue loop and a second 8-residue loop.
source: The domains are connected by two loops: one 9-residue loop that runs from β4 in domain A to β5 in domain B, and a second 8-residue loop that connects β9 in domain B and β10 in domain A.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The two long loops connecting the domains of BstB could work as a hinge to allow a bending motion of two domains to induce a conformational change upon substrate binding.
source: These two long loops could work as a hinge to allow a bending motion of two domains to induce a conformational change upon substrate binding; this is often observed with SBPs/PBPs (de Boer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural features and comparison to known SBP/PBP behavior.

claim: An α-helix formed by the C-terminal residues of BstB lies behind the cleft and may allow flexibility of the two domains.
source: In addition, an α-helix formed by the C-terminal residues lies behind the cleft and may also allow flexibility of the two domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural features.

claim: Several extended loops in BstB exhibit poor electron densities, suggesting conformational sampling of more than one state.
source: Several extend loops are found on the domain-domain interface. The loops (residues 34–38 and residues 171–177) exhibit poor electron densities, suggesting conformational sampling of more than one state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on crystallographic data quality.

claim: The cleft between domains A and B of BstB forms a bulky cavity with an area of ~1179.5 Å2 and a volume of ~1009.6 Å3.
source: The cleft between domains A and B forms a bulky cavity with an area of ~1179.5 Å2 and a volume of ~1009.6 Å3 that extends into domain A and is only accessible to solvent from one side of the structure.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The cavity in BstB is predominantly hydrophobic, suggesting large and hydrophobic substrates like sterols are favorable for binding.
source: The cavity is predominantly hydrophobic, suggesting large and hydrophobic substrates like sterols are favorable for binding (Figure 4B, Table 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the hydrophobic nature of the cavity.

claim: A second pocket in BstB (area of ~172 Å2; volume of ~117 Å3) is found in domain B and close to the central cleft.
source: Additionally, a second pocket (area of ~172 Å2; volume of ~117 Å3) is found in domain B and close to the central cleft.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The second pocket in BstB is localized behind the unmodeled loop (residues 202–204), with the extremely poor density in this part implying high flexibility.
source: This pocket is localized behind the unmodeled loop (residues 202–204), with the extremely poor density in this part implying high flexibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on crystallographic data quality.

claim: The second pocket in BstB is highly hydrophobic, but its role (if any) in ligand binding is unexplored.
source: This pocket is highly hydrophobic, but its role (if any) in ligand binding is unexplored (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the function of this structural feature.

claim: A DALI structural homology search suggests the structure of BstB closely resembles that of PBPs that share a bi-lobe architecture and undergo conformational change upon substrate binding to the central cavity.
source: A DALI structural homology search (Holm and Rosenström, 2010) suggests the structure of BstB closely resembles that of PBPs that share a bi-lobe architecture and undergo conformational change upon substrate binding to the central cavity (Quiocho and Ledvina, 1996).
evidence: This is based on computational structural comparison supported by citations.

claim: BstB adopts an intermediate conformation between the unliganded PhnD and liganded PhnD.
source: The comparison revealed that BstB adopts an intermediate conformation between the unliganded PhnD (3S4U) and liganded one (3P7I, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis.

claim: The cleft in BstB is less open (~10 Å) than that in apo-PhnD (~22 Å).
source: The cleft in BstB is less open (~10 Å) than that in apo-PhnD (~22 Å).
evidence: This is based on structural measurements and comparison.

claim: In the docking model, the 4-monomethyl sterol was positioned in the hydrophobic cavity in domain A with the polar head pointing toward the central cleft and domain B.
source: In the first iteration, the protein was held rigid, and the ligand allowed to dock flexibly. In this docking model, the sterol was positioned in the hydrophobic cavity in domain A with the polar head pointing toward the central cleft and domain B, adjacent to three residues: Glu118, Tyr120, and Asn192.
evidence: This describes the results of computational docking studies.

claim: There are three energetically favored poses for 4-monomethyl sterol binding to BstB: two form a single hydrogen bond to Tyr120, while one forms two hydrogen bonds to Tyr120 and Asn192.
source: There are three energetically favored poses: two (MonoA and MonoB) form a single hydrogen bond to Tyr120, while pose MonoC where the hydroxyl makes two hydrogen bonds to Tyr120 and Asn192 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C, Table 5).
evidence: This describes the results of computational docking studies.

claim: In the three poses where there was initially an interaction with Tyr120, that interaction is lost during MD simulation and replaced with a new hydrogen bond with Glu118, which persists for 85–95% of the simulation.
source: In the three poses where there was initially an interaction with Tyr120, that interaction is lost and replaced with a new hydrogen bond with Glu118, which persists for 85–95% of the simulation.
evidence: This describes the results of molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The 4,4-dimethyl sterol showed interesting behavior during the 20 ns simulations, with different poses retaining or losing hydrogen bonds.
source: The 4,4-dimethyl sterol showed interesting behavior during the 20 ns simulations. Pose DiA, which had three hydrogen bonds after ICM-Pro docking, retained all three interactions (although those with Glu118 and Tyr120 are intermittent and persist for only 12% of the simulation). Pose DiB retained both interactions from the docking model, although the hydrogen bond to Tyr120 was only present for 10% of the simulation. The third pose, DiC, showed the largest structural changes, losing the one interaction it had with Tyr120.
evidence: This describes the results of molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The differences in hydrogen bonding behavior between monomethyl and dimethyl sterols, although subtle, may explain the reduction in affinity for the dimethyl sterol substrate.
source: It is possible that these differences, although subtle, explain the reduction in affinity for the dimethyl sterol substrate.
evidence: This is speculation based on the MD simulation results.

claim: The aliphatic tails of all docked sterols reside in a hydrophobic cavity in domain A lined by specific residues.
source: The aliphatic tails of all docked sterols reside in a hydrophobic cavity in domain A lined by the side chains of Tyr33, Pro34, Ala46, Met47, Met50, Ile89, Ser91, Leu92, Pro110, Ile112, Leu219, Met220, Val222, Leu244, Leu253, Cys254, Phe257, Ile259, and Phe262 in domain A.
evidence: This describes the results of docking studies.

claim: Sequence alignment shows that residues lining the hydrophobic cavity are highly conserved between proteins in the same SSN cluster, implying their significance in forming the substrate binding pocket.
source: Sequence alignment shows that these residues are highly conserved between proteins in the same SSN cluster, implying their significance in forming the substrate binding pocket.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Mutagenesis to remove or reduce the potential interactions with the polar head and the aliphatic tail showed subtle influences (<twofold) on the sterol binding affinity.
source: Mutagenesis to remove or reduce the potential interactions with the polar head and the aliphatic tail showed subtle influences (<twofold) on the sterol binding affinity, indicating that the interaction between the protein and sterol is extensive and principally depends on hydrophobic interactions that are not easily disrupted (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on experimental mutagenesis data.

claim: The interaction between BstB and sterol is extensive and principally depends on hydrophobic interactions that are not easily disrupted.
source: Mutagenesis to remove or reduce the potential interactions with the polar head and the aliphatic tail showed subtle influences (<twofold) on the sterol binding affinity, indicating that the interaction between the protein and sterol is extensive and principally depends on hydrophobic interactions that are not easily disrupted (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on mutagenesis results.

claim: A 150 ns molecular dynamics simulation on apo-BstB showed that at ~90 ns there was a distinct conformational change in the structure.
source: To investigate whether BstB can undergo conformational change (as most PBPs do upon substrate binding), a 150 ns molecular dynamics simulation on apo-BstB was performed (Video 1). Plotting the RMSD of the simulated structure against the initial crystal structure at 25 ps intervals during the MD trajectory shows that for the first ~90 ns the protein showed some degree of flexibility (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A). During this part of the trajectory, the RMSD oscillates between 2.0 and 3.1 Å (average RMSD = 2.6 Å). At ~90 ns, there was a distinct conformational change in the structure giving rise to conformations with RMSDs ranging from 2.7 to 4.5 (average RMSD = 3.3 Å).
evidence: This describes the results of molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Visual analysis of the MD trajectory shows that at ~90 ns the two domains of BstB open by approximately 20°.
source: Visual analysis of the MD trajectory shows that at ~90 ns the two domains open by approximately 20° (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B, Video 1).
evidence: This describes the results of molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The simulation on the MonoC docked complex did not show the same conformational change as the apo-BstB simulation, which supports the idea that the apo-BstB structure represents a 'partially-open' form of the protein.
source: In contrast, the simulation (150 ns) on the MonoC docked complex which had a RMSD of 2.6 Å for the entire length of the trajectory and did not show the same conformational change as the apo-BstB simulation, which supports the idea that the apo-BstB structure represents a 'partially-open' form of the protein (Video 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing MD simulations of apo and ligand-bound forms.

claim: The structure of BstC was determined by experimental phasing to a resolution of 1.9 Å.
source: The structure of BstC was also determined by experimental phasing to a resolution of 1.9 Å.
evidence: This describes the crystallographic structure determination.

claim: Two monomers in the asymmetric unit of BstC form a dimer with 180 rotational symmetry.

evidence: This describes structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Each monomer of BstC adopts an all-α-helical structure with 12 α-helices in total.
source: Each monomer adopts an all-α-helical structure with 12 α-helices in total, designated with H1 to H12; 9 antiparallel arranged helices (H4-H12) form an irregular ring with a pore running through the center.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Nine antiparallel arranged helices (H4-H12) in BstC form an irregular ring with a pore running through the center.
source: Each monomer adopts an all-α-helical structure with 12 α-helices in total, designated with H1 to H12; 9 antiparallel arranged helices (H4-H12) form an irregular ring with a pore running through the center.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: BstC has a predominantly hydrophilic exterior surface.
source: Hydrophobicity analysis shows that BstC has a predominantly hydrophilic exterior surface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Three cavities are found in the center of the BstC structure, annotated as Tunnel 1 (TN1), Cavity 1 (CA1) and Cavity 2 (CA2), with total area of ~597.1 Å2 and total volume of ~447 Å3.
source: Three cavities are found in the center of the structure. We annotated them as Tunnel 1 (TN1), Cavity 1 (CA1) and Cavity 2 (CA2), with total area of ~597.1 Å2 and total volume of ~447 Å3.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: TN1 in BstC exhibits a mixture of hydrophobic and hydrophilic amino acids.
source: TN1 is closer to the N-terminal face of the structure, while CA1 and CA2 are proximal to the C-terminal face and form two open hydrophobic pockets; TN1 exhibits a mixture of hydrophobic and hydrophilic amino acids (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Table 6).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The extensive hydrophobic environment inside the BstC structure suggests it can accommodate large hydrophobic substrates.
source: The extensive hydrophobic environment inside the BstC structure suggests it can accommodate large hydrophobic substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hydrophobic nature of the cavities.

claim: Most of the surface of BstC, especially the C-terminal face, exhibits strong negative charge.
source: Notably, electrostatic calculation shows that most of the surface of BstC, especially the C-terminal face, exhibits strong negative charge (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on computational electrostatic analysis of the structure.

claim: The charged surfaces of BstC may mediate protein-protein interactions, perhaps with BstB.
source: These charged surfaces may mediate protein-protein interactions, perhaps with BstB.
evidence: This is speculation based on the electrostatic properties of the surface.

source: A structure similarity search using the DALI server revealed high homology to Tp0956 (PDB 3U64, Treponema pallidum strain Nichols).
evidence: This is based on computational structural comparison.

source: Tp0956 is the T-component protein of a subfamily of TRAP (tripartite ATP-independent periplasmic) transporters known as TPATs (tetratricopeptide repeat-protein associated TRAP transporters), which are implicated in the transport of organic acid ligands in bacteria (Brautigam et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The true physiological substrate of Tp0956 has not been determined.
source: The true physiological substrate of Tp0956 has not been determined, but Treponema is a spirochete known to rely on import of host lipids and fatty acids to construct its cell envelope (Radolf et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the state of knowledge about Tp0956.

claim: Treponema is a spirochete known to rely on import of host lipids and fatty acids to construct its cell envelope.
source: The true physiological substrate of Tp0956 has not been determined, but Treponema is a spirochete known to rely on import of host lipids and fatty acids to construct its cell envelope (Radolf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Tp0956 contains four helical hairpins that are similar to tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motifs, which are hallmarks of proteins that are involved in protein-protein interactions.
source: Tp0956 contains four helical hairpins that are similar to tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motifs, which are hallmarks of proteins that are involved in protein-protein interactions (D'Andrea and Regan, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The TPR-like substructure is also observed in BstC and forms part of the pore and lateral surface of the protein, hinting that BstC might engage with itself or other proteins.

evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: SEC-MALS analysis shows that the purified BstC exists both as a monomer and a dimer in solution with a ratio ~3:1.

claim: The role of the dimerization in BstC is not clear and its determination will require additional studies.
source: However, the role of the dimerization in this protein is not clear and its determination will require additional studies.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the functional significance of dimerization.

claim: All the sterols were found embedded in the hydrophobic cavity (CA1) of BstC in docking models, with the hydroxyl group pointing inwards and the aliphatic tail pointed out.
source: All the sterols were found embedded in the hydrophobic cavity (CA1) lined by Gly128, Val131, Arg132, Met135, Ala138, Leu139, Leu142, Leu145, Leu167, Met170, Leu171, Lys174, Ala175, Pro176, and Phe208, with the hydroxyl group pointing inwards and the aliphatic tail pointed out (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–B).

claim: Residues involved in sterol interaction in BstC are located on H6, H7, H8 and H10 and are all highly conserved in a sequence alignment of the closest BstC homologs.
source: Residues involved in sterol interaction are located on H6, H7, H8 and H10 and are all highly conserved in a sequence alignment of the closest BstC homologs.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: MD simulations reveal that the 4-monomethyl sterol substrate moves approximately 8–9 Å further into the binding site of BstC and the polar head makes a hydrogen bonding contact with the side chain of Glu86.
source: We then performed multiple 20 ns molecular dynamics simulations on the docked models of 4-monomethyl sterol from ICM-Pro. The simulations reveal that the substrate moves approximately 8–9 Å further into the binding site and the polar head makes a hydrogen bonding contact with the side chain of Glu86 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes the results of molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The hydrogen bond between 4-monomethyl sterol and Glu86 in BstC persists for 94% of the total simulation time.
source: This movement takes place almost immediately and the hydrogen bond persists for 94% of the total time.
evidence: This describes the results of molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Simulations with the 4,4-dimethyl sterol revealed that it behaves differently in BstC in that it moves slowly inwards and does not get as deep (~2.6 Å) into the pocket as the monomethyl sterol.
source: Intriguingly, simulations with the 4,4-dimethyl sterol revealed that it behaves differently in that it moves slowly inwards and does not get as deep (~2.6 Å) into the pocket as the monomethyl sterol (Figure 5 – figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This describes the results of molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: A water-mediated contact is formed between the 4,4-dimethyl sterol polar head and the side chain of Glu86 in BstC but persists for only 2% of the simulation time.
source: A water-mediated contact is formed between the polar head and the side chain of Glu86 but persist for only 2% of the time.
evidence: This describes the results of molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The lack of additional movement and H-bonding interaction of 4,4-dimethyl sterol in BstC may explain the binding data, where the protein has a Kd for the monomethyl sterol that is ~30 × lower than for the dimethyl sterol substrate.
source: This lack of additional movement and H-bonding interaction may explain the binding data, where the protein has a Kd for the monomethyl sterol that is ~30 × lower than for the dimethyl sterol substrate.
evidence: This is an inference connecting simulation results to experimental binding data.

claim: Mutagenesis to convert Glu86 to Gly and Trp in BstC leads to ~4.5 and 100-fold decrease in the equilibrium affinity for 4-monomethyl sterol.
source: Mutagenesis to convert Glu86 to Gly and Trp to remove or reduce the potential interactions with the polar head of the sterols leads to ~4.5 and 100-fold decrease in the equilibrium affinity for 4-monomethyl sterol (Figure 5—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is based on experimental mutagenesis data.

claim: The mutagenesis of Glu86 in BstC eliminates the binding to 4,4-dimethyl sterol, cholesterol and lanosterol.
source: Meanwhile, the mutagenesis eliminates the binding to 4,4-dimethyl sterol, cholesterol and lanosterol (Figure 5—figure supplement 6B and C).
evidence: This is based on experimental mutagenesis data.

claim: Glu86 plays a critical role in interacting with and stabilizing the sterols in BstC.
source: These findings indicate that Glu86 plays a critical role in interacting with and stabilizing the sterols.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis results.

claim: The most-studied family of lipid transfer proteins in mammals is the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR)-related lipid transfer (START) domain (STARD) proteins.
source: The most-studied family in mammals is the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR)-related lipid transfer (START) domain (STARD) proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian lipid transfer proteins.

claim: All fifteen STARD proteins identified to date possess lipid-harboring START domains that can be divided into six subfamilies based on sequence similarity and ligand specificity.
source: All fifteen STARD proteins identified to date possess lipid-harboring START domains that can be divided into six subfamilies based on sequence similarity and ligand specificity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about STARD proteins.

claim: The GRAMD1s/Lam/Ltc family was shown to mediate non-vesicular sterol transport from the plasma membrane to the endoplasmic reticulum to maintain sterol homeostasis.
source: In addition to STARD proteins, a novel yet evolutionarily conserved family that contains the START-like domains called the GRAMD1s/Lam/Ltc family (GRAMD1s in mammals and Lam/Ltc in yeast) was shown to mediate non-vesicular sterol transport from the plasma membrane to the endoplasmic reticulum to maintain sterol homeostasis (Gatta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The Osh/ORP/OSBP proteins are considered to be either sterol-sensing and/or sterol-transfer proteins.
source: A third family consists of the Osh/ORP/OSBP proteins (Oxysterol-binding homology in yeast and Oxysterol-binding Protein/OSBP-Related Protein in mammals), which are considered to be either sterol-sensing and/or sterol-transfer proteins (Raychaudhuri and Prinz, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Two Niemann-Pick type C proteins, NPC1 and NPC2, were reported to directly bind and transport cholesterols and various oxysterols.
source: Besides these, two Niemann-Pick type C proteins, NPC1 and NPC2, were also reported to directly bind and transport cholesterols and various oxysterols; defective NPC proteins causes NPC disease, a fetal neurodegenerative disorder where sterols aberrantly accumulate in the lysosome (Carstea et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Defective NPC proteins cause NPC disease, a fetal neurodegenerative disorder where sterols aberrantly accumulate in the lysosome.
source: Besides these, two Niemann-Pick type C proteins, NPC1 and NPC2, were also reported to directly bind and transport cholesterols and various oxysterols; defective NPC proteins causes NPC disease, a fetal neurodegenerative disorder where sterols aberrantly accumulate in the lysosome (Carstea et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The comparative analysis shows that the eukaryotic sterol transporters share very little resemblance with BstB and BstC.
source: Our comparative analysis shows that the eukaryotic sterol transporters share very little resemblance with BstB and BstC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparison analysis.

claim: The bilobed architecture of BstB is pronounced in its divergence from eukaryotic sterol transporters, suggesting that this protein evolved separately and may work in a distinct manner.
source: The bilobed architecture of BstB is pronounced in its divergence from eukaryotic sterol transporters, suggesting that this protein evolved separately and may work in a distinct manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: For the all-helical BstC, the only similarities with eukaryotic sterol transporters are the presence of a hydrophobic tunnel formed in the center of the protein that can accommodate sterols, and a loop next to the tunnel's entrance that may be used as a 'lid'.
source: For the all-helical BstC, the only similarities are the presence of a hydrophobic tunnel formed in the center of the protein that can accommodate sterols, and a loop next to the tunnel's entrance that may also be used as a 'lid' to restrict access to the substrate binding site (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis.

claim: Bioinformatic analyses revealed that BstA, BstB, and BstC belong to well-studied families of bacterial metabolite transporters.
source: Bioinformatic analyses revealed that BstA, BstB, and BstC belong to well-studied families of bacterial metabolite transporters.
evidence: This is a summary of bioinformatic analysis results.

claim: High resolution structures of BstB and BstC show that their large ligand binding sites display a dichotomy of hydrophobic and hydrophilic amino acids whose sidechains interact with the sterol hydrophobic tail and hydrophilic head.
source: High resolution structures of BstB and BstC show that their large ligand binding sites display a dichotomy of hydrophobic and hydrophilic amino acids whose sidechains interact with the sterol hydrophobic tail and hydrophilic head.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and docking studies.

claim: The Bst proteins share sequence and structural homology with bacterial transporters involved in the trafficking of essential nutrients such as sugars, amino acids, vitamins, solutes, and metal ions.
source: In summary, the Bst proteins share sequence and structural homology with bacterial transporters involved in the trafficking of essential nutrients such as sugars, amino acids, vitamins, solutes, and metal ions (Davidson et al., 2008; Higgins, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The implication of Bst proteins in the transport of sterols expands the substrate repertoire for their respective families.
source: Their implication in the transport of sterols expands the substrate repertoire for their respective families.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the significance of the findings.

claim: The substrate binding sites detected in BstB and BstC should now enable the curation of functionally homologous sites in bacterial proteins, including in those from human pathogens known to traffic host lipids.
source: The substrate binding sites detected in BstB and BstC should now enable the curation of functionally homologous sites in bacterial proteins, including in those from human pathogens known to traffic host lipids.
